Day 79 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Persistent Storage

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and StorageClasses separate application data from the lifecycle of individual Pods.

Architecture / mental model

Pod → PVC → PV → storage backend
          ↑
     StorageClass / provisioner

How it works

A PersistentVolume is cluster storage whose lifecycle is independent of an individual Pod. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a workload's request for storage, and a StorageClass can define how compatible storage is provisioned dynamically.

A claim typically declares an access mode, storage request and optionally a `storageClassName`. With a suitable class, the claim can trigger dynamic provisioning; otherwise a compatible PV must exist for binding.

The Pod references the PVC by name and mounts that volume into the container. The controller can replace the Pod while the claim remains connected to persistent data.

Hands-on reference

kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get pv
kubectl describe pvc app-data
kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RECLAIM:.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy

Verification

Create a PVC and Pod, write data, replace the Pod and prove the new Pod sees the same data. Inspect PVC events and binding state rather than waiting at `Pending` with spiritual optimism.

Field note / gotcha

`ReadWriteOnce` means read-write mounting by a single node, not necessarily a single Pod. `ReadWriteOncePod` is the access mode intended for true single-Pod access when the driver supports it.

Security considerations

Review the StorageClass, reclaim policy and backend encryption/access controls. Persistent storage survives workload replacement, so sensitive data can outlive the process that created it.

What I learned

Compute can be disposable without forcing application state to share the same lifecycle.
